extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and university mathematics instructors (researchers in mathematics education)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical analysis of what functions proofs should serve in introductory university mathematics courses, based on interviews with ten mathematicians; focuses particularly on the 'transfer' function (proofs as vehicles for methods/techniques useful elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer (proofs as carriers of methods and techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs introduce new techniques, important concepts and exercise in logical reasoning needed in problem solving; proofs can 'introduce new techniques to attack other problems' and 'offer understanding for something different from the original context'. The authors label this function 'transfer'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples mentioned: completing the square (used beyond deriving quadratic formula), Archimedes' method (heuristic that generalises), and proofs that demonstrate techniques that can be copied to other problems. The paper stresses studying learners' constructions of similarity across proving and problem solving when aiming for transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction (proofs that convince)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs provide conviction: they present convincing arguments for statements, especially those not evident to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians stressed presenting proofs or convincing arguments for statements 'which are not conceived as evident by the students' to enable students to experience the function of conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation (proofs that explain relationships between concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs explain how mathematical concepts are related and thereby promote understanding beyond rule application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper links this to the function of explanation: proof is said to 'explain how the concepts are related to each other' and contrasts university proof with school mathematics' rule-application approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of definitions and axiomatic structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs serve to justify the use of particular definitions or an axiomatic framework (Weber, 2002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proofs are distinct from those that merely verify results; they show why certain definitions or axioms are appropriate and useful in the mathematical system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration of proving techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs can explicitly illustrate proof techniques that are useful in other proving situations (distinct but related to transfer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weber (2002) and the interviewed mathematicians note that certain proofs exemplify techniques students can apply elsewhere; teachers should highlight the technique as an object of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification (proof as backbone of mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs verify results and thereby provide the foundational backbone of mathematics; 'without proof "everything will collapse"'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians referenced this verification function as a reason to include proof in curricula — one cannot proceed in mathematics without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual challenge and engagement (aha-experiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs provide intellectual challenge, curiosity and 'aha-experiences' that motivate students to learn more about proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One mathematician emphasised that proof enhances students' interest; prior work showed about 80% of entrants wanted to learn more about proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic value (presenting 'beautiful proofs')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs are valuable because of their aesthetic qualities ('beautiful proofs'), which can be pedagogically useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematician noted the importance of presenting beautiful proofs when possible, though suitable examples for basic courses may be hard to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and learning mathematical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs help students learn mathematical language and modes of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One respondent highlighted proof as useful for learning mathematical language; proofs serve communicative functions in the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice in logical reasoning and problem-solving skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying proofs habituates students to mathematical reasoning and logical argumentation, skills transferable to problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians wrote that being accustomed to studying proofs 'practices' mathematical reasoning; quotes emphasise logical reasoning as useful across contexts (including engineering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of proof (how and how much to focus on proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about how visible the artifact of proof should be to learners — 'the condition of transparency' — i.e., how and how much to focus on various aspects and functions of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers must choose whether to foreground proof as proof or use proofs implicitly in doing mathematics; transparency affects students' capacity to see proofs' roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-adjusted rigor and selection of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and adapt the amount and formality of proof to the audience (e.g., applied/engineering students may need fewer or less rigorous proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mathematicians advocated 'serving up' mathematics with as few proofs as possible for applied students and concentrating on applications; others argued for at least some proofs to develop reasoning skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demystify proving by treating proving and problem solving as related activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Present proving as part of general mathematical reasoning (calculation/problem solving) to demystify proofs for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several mathematicians stated they consider proving and problem solving as 'in principle the same activity' and suggested teaching proofs as concentrated forms of reasoning or calculation to reduce student fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of open tasks to promote investigation and hypothesis formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Open tasks encourage willingness to investigate, make hypotheses, and then prove or disprove them — fostering habits useful in proving tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open tasks were explicitly recommended as exercises that stimulate investigative behaviour and subsequent proof/refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific elementary proofs as exemplars for transferable techniques and concept consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary and central proofs in basic courses serve as concrete vehicles to teach techniques and consolidate concepts (e.g., induction, proof by contradiction, irrationality of √2, divisibility proofs, refutation via counterexample, derivative proofs, factor theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists examples and how they transfer: induction (Pascal's triangle), contradiction (infinitely many primes), irrationality of √2 (generalisable), n(n+1) divisible by 2 (divisibility techniques), tasks about P(x) and counterexamples (understanding what a refutation requires), derivative proofs (consolidate limit/difference quotient), factor theorem (proof gives extra information about remainder). Teachers are advised to use these as models of techniques/concepts that students can apply elsewhere.
